the tax form asks for 'declaration of any capital gains realized', do i have to say something about selling my phone

The tax form you mentioned is asking whether you sold assets like stocks or property that made a profit, not everyday items like your phone. Since you are the only one who knows if that phone was an investment or just personal stuff you used, you should decide based on your own situation. If you are unsure whether your phone sale counts as a capital gain for the IRS, you might want to ask them directly instead of guessing.
the contract says the agreement is 'subject to contract', does that mean it isn't official yet

That phrase means the deal you signed isn't actually binding right now because the final agreement still needs to be fully written up and agreed on by everyone. Until that final version is signed, you are not yet officially locked in to the terms of the contract. Since I cannot see the specific papers you have, you should contact the other side of the agreement to ask exactly when that last version will be ready.
the form asks for my 'filing status', what box do i check for my taxes

"Filing status" on your tax form simply means picking the category that best describes your personal and family situation for the year. You should check the box on the form that matches whether you are single, married, or head of a household, since choosing the wrong one can change how much tax you owe or get back. If you are unsure which category fits your life, the best next step is to ask a tax professional who can review your specific details.
how much tax will I pay on 32000 a year

The form you are looking at is the tax year's Income Tax calculation, which figures out how much of that 32,000 yearly amount the government keeps versus what you get to keep. Because the exact amount depends on your personal allowances and where you live, I cannot give you a specific number or do the math for you. You will need to ask the tax office or a qualified accountant to run the official numbers on your specific situation.
my bank letter says my account is 'overdrawn', what does that mean

An overdrawn account means you have spent more money than is actually sitting in there, so you owe the bank some cash. You will likely need to put money in soon to bring the balance back up to zero or pay off the amount you are short.
my landlord's email says the tenancy will 'roll onto a periodic basis', what does that mean

That phrase from your landlord's email means your fixed-term contract is ending, and your rent will now be collected month-to-month as if there were no end date. Since I cannot see the specific dates or terms in your agreement, you should ask your landlord exactly how much notice you need to give to move out and what the current rent amount is.
the insurance quote mentions 'excess may vary depending on the claim history', what part of my history counts

That quote means the extra amount you pay if a claim happens isn't fixed; it changes based on your past insurance claims. The specific part of your history that counts is usually only your recent record, but the exact time period and types of claims the insurer checks depend on their own rules. Since I cannot see your personal file, you should contact the insurance company directly to ask which years of your history they are looking at.

the loan paperwork mentions a 'default', what happens if i stop making my monthly payments

In your loan paperwork, a "default" simply means you have missed enough payments that the lender considers the loan seriously broken. If you stop paying your monthly installments now, this will happen, and it can lead to your name being marked as in debt, extra fees being added, or even legal action against you. You should contact your lender directly right away to see if there are options to talk about, but I cannot tell you the exact consequences for your specific account.
how many hours are included if the package says up to fifty per month

That package means you are allowed to use up to fifty hours of service during any month. It doesn't give you a fixed total, so you simply won't be able to go over that limit in the billing period. I cannot calculate how many hours you have left because I cannot see your personal usage records, so you will need to check your account directly or ask the support team.
my letter says i must 'comply with the terms and conditions of the lease', does that just mean follow the rules

That phrase on your letter means you must follow the specific rules written in your lease agreement. It asks you to make sure you are doing everything required there, like paying rent on time or keeping the property clean. If you are unsure which rule you might be breaking, you should ask your landlord or the agent who sent the letter. I cannot tell you exactly what those rules are without seeing your actual document.
the parking notice says 'representations must be made within the statutory period', what are they asking

They are asking you to submit any complaints or questions about that parking notice before the official deadline set by the law, which is known as the statutory period. You need to check the date on the notice itself to see if you still have time to reply, since I cannot see the specific dates listed there. If you are unsure whether you are still within that legal window, you should contact the authority that issued the notice for clarification.
can you explain what an escrow account is on a loan without the bank terminology

An escrow account is simply a holding box where a separate manager keeps your money for specific bills like property taxes and home insurance so the bank doesn't have to manage them directly. You will likely see this requested on your monthly mortgage statement, and it means you should expect a little extra added to your regular payment to cover those costs when they come due. Since I cannot see your specific loan details or calculate your exact balance, you should check the breakdown on your official statement or ask your lender to explain how much is being set aside for you.
what does it mean to be self-employed compared with employed

Being employed usually means you work for a boss who pays your wages and handles things like taxes, whereas being self-employed means you run your own business and are responsible for filing your own taxes and managing your own schedule. The difference matters because if you are employed, your employer deducts tax automatically from your pay, but if you are self-employed, you must set aside money from your income to pay these bills on your own. Since your specific situation depends on how you are classified for tax purposes, you should check the details on your actual employment contract or consult a tax professional to confirm which category applies to you.

Since the exact details depend on the specific order you have in hand, you should check the deadline and instructions printed on that document or ask the sender for clarification.
